analysis.one_liner: Lets any American buy into Medicare's health insurance program at cost.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 82 Democratic cosponsors in March 2010, the bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have opened Medicare — the government health insurance program that people 65 and older already use — to any U.S. citizen or legal permanent resident who wanted to buy into it. Premiums would be set to cover the actual cost of care within each age group, so the program would pay for itself rather than rely on taxpayer subsidies. It sat in the Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone without affordable health coverage — the uninsured, people priced out of private plans, and those with pre-existing conditions that private insurers could refuse or charge heavily for before the 2010 health law fully took effect. They would gain a public insurance option priced at the government's actual cost, with no shareholders or marketing overhead built into the premium.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The uninsured and people priced out of private plans

how_it_helps.text: Every U.S. citizen and legal permanent resident would become eligible to enroll in Medicare's insurance program, not just people 65 and older [S3].
Premiums would be calculated by age group so that each cohort's members cover their own care costs, rather than depending on general taxpayer funding [S3].
Coverage could not take effect before the first calendar year after enactment, giving the program time to set up enrollment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers would lose any customers who switched to the public program, and their individual-market business model would face direct price competition from a plan that does not need to turn a profit. Taxpayers would bear little direct cost, since premiums are designed to cover the program's own expenses.

drawbacks.text: The bill provides no subsidies: enrollees pay the full premium themselves, and because premiums must cover costs within each age group, older enrollees (56-64) and families could face premiums that remain expensive relative to income [S3].
Coverage would not begin until at least the first calendar year after enactment, so it would not have helped anyone immediately [S3].
It would draw healthier and sicker customers into an age-based pool with no risk adjustment across cohorts, which could push premiums higher for people with serious medical needs in each age band.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people the private market failed, a Medicare buy-in at cost would have been a genuine safety net with essentially no taxpayer price tag. Its honest weakness is affordability: without subsidies it helps the most only those who can already pay a real premium, and its age-cohort pricing could still be steep for older workers. It was a serious but self-funded design, not a free universal program.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, got sent to a health subcommittee a week later, and stayed there with no markup or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced March 9, 2010 with 82 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee [S1] [S5].
On March 18, 2010 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where it remained; the committee never reported it out and the House never voted on it [S5].
The 111th Congress ended January 3, 2011 without the bill advancing past committee referral [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers were better off: they faced no public plan competing on price in the individual market, and the Affordable Care Act enacted three weeks later still routed new coverage expansion through private insurance plans.

for.name: Rep. Alan Grayson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 82 Democratic cosponsors, all within three days of introduction.

for.name: 82 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the support of about a third of the House majority at introduction.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Sander Levin (D)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on March 9, 2010, sent it to a health subcommittee, and never marked it up or reported it to the House.

against.name: Speaker Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: In the same weeks, brought the Affordable Care Act to the floor without a public option provision; H.R. 4789 received no floor consideration.

sides.party_line_note: All 82 cosponsors were Democrats, roughly a third of the 253-member Democratic House majority; no Republican cosponsor appears in the record [S4].

industries.note: A Medicare buy-in at cost would have let individuals buy insurance directly from the government, competing on price with private plans that carry marketing and profit margins. Insurers would lose policyholders, so their interest ran against the uninsured and overpriced-plan customers this bill served.
Employees with a buy-in option could leave employer plans, which could relieve some firms of premiums but risk leaving plans with a sicker, more expensive pool of remaining workers.
